title: Vance Walks Back 'Indentured Servants' Remark After India's Strong Protest
excerpt: At a CBS News town hall, JD Vance said his rhetoric was imperfect and that his criticism targeted US companies and the H-1B system, not visa holders — while stressing that the PERM suspensions stand separately from H-1B status.
body:
• US Vice President JD Vance said his rhetoric was "imperfect" and that calling H-1B workers "indentured servants" was not a criticism of the visa holders themselves.
  • Vance said his target was US companies and a visa system that ties a worker's legal status to one employer, giving that employer too much power.
  • India's Ministry of External Affairs had called the term "deeply offensive," saying it carried painful historical and colonial connotations and overlooked Indian professionals' contributions to the US economy.
  • The clarification changes no rule: the PERM suspension affecting eight companies is separate from H-1B status, and existing H-1B visas and holders' dependants are not invalidated by it, according to the MEA.

US Vice President JD Vance has walked back his description of H-1B workers as "indentured servants," acknowledging at a CBS News town hall on Saturday that his rhetoric had been imperfect and that his criticism was aimed at American companies and the visa system, not at the workers themselves.

Vance was responding to a question from an Indian immigrant who became a US citizen five years ago and voted for President Donald Trump, according to The Times of India and YourStory. "I would say, and to the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said.

What Vance Said He Meant

Vance argued that an H-1B worker's legal status is closely tied to a sponsoring company, which certifies it cannot find an alternative American applicant, while the worker's visa is often their only lifeline to the United States. That dependence, he said, gives employers excessive control.

"So, when I say indentured servitude, that is not a criticism of H1B visa holders; that is the criticism of the company, which brings a person who sometimes will lay off an American worker and knows that if they complain, if they have disagreement with the boss, they could just lose their job."

— JD Vance, US Vice President

He added that his goal was not to dehumanise immigrants, pointed to his own family, and said the United States needed to balance welcoming foreign professionals with protecting American workers. His wife, Second Lady Usha Vance, is the daughter of Indian immigrants. "You know where my family comes from, and I love my mother-in-law and father-in-law who immigrated from South India," he said.

India's Protest

The clarification followed a strong objection from India's Ministry of External Affairs, which called the description "unwarranted" and said it overlooked Indian professionals' contributions to the US economy. "Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the MEA said, adding that talent mobility benefits both countries.

The MEA also drew a line that matters directly to workers caught up in the current enforcement action: the US decision to suspend certain companies from the Permanent Labour Certification, or PERM, programme is separate from the H-1B programme. The suspension could affect the green card process for eligible employees of those companies, but it does not by itself invalidate existing H-1B visas or change the status of visa holders and their dependants.

The Remarks That Started the Row

Earlier this month, at a news conference on visa fraud, Vance described H-1B workers as "indentured servants" and accused foreign outsourcing firms of bringing in employees at lower wages while laying off American workers. He claimed H-1B workers earned $20,000 less than American citizens in similar positions, and workers brought in by foreign outsourcing firms earned $48,000 less. The administration subsequently suspended eight companies — TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe — from the PERM programme.

PERM is an early step in the employment-based green card process. As the US Department of Labor's PERM page explains, the department must certify that there are not sufficient US workers able, willing, qualified and available for the job. Workers can review H-1B requirements on the USCIS H-1B specialty occupations page.

What This Means for H-1B Holders

Indian professionals account for more than 70 per cent of approved H-1B petitions annually, so the language used about the programme in Washington lands directly on the largest group in it. Vance's clarification does not reverse the PERM suspensions, change any wage claim he made, or alter H-1B rules. What it does is separate, in the administration's own words, the workers from the system being criticised — a distinction India's protest demanded and that employers and workers will cite as the debate over the programme continues.

For holders employed by a suspended company, the practical position remains the one the MEA stated: an H-1B visa stays valid, while a future green card step that depends on that employer's PERM filing is the part at risk — worth confirming with the employer's immigration counsel before making job or travel decisions on the headlines alone.
